track.name: bankruptcy-law
track.label: Bankruptcy & Insolvency Law
track.summary: The legal mechanics behind every restructuring: the Chapter 11 process end-to-end, the specific Bankruptcy Code sections that actually drive deal terms, creditor priority fights, and how restructuring advisors work alongside counsel.

phases.title: Foundations of Bankruptcy Law
phases.description: Learn what actually happens the moment a company files: the automatic stay that freezes creditor action, how Chapters 7, 11, and 15 differ in practice, and the roles of everyone in the room — debtor's counsel, the UCC, the U.S. Trustee, and the judge.

phases.title: The Chapter 11 Process End-to-End
phases.description: Walk the case from the first-day motions filed within hours of a petition through DIP financing negotiations to the plan of reorganization and disclosure statement that ultimately gets confirmed.

phases.title: Key Legal Mechanisms Every Analyst Should Recognize
phases.description: Go deep on the specific Bankruptcy Code sections that drive deal terms in practice: Section 365 executory contracts and leases, Section 363 asset sales, and Sections 547/548 preference and fraudulent transfer actions.

phases.title: Creditor Rights and Priority Fights
phases.description: Master the absolute priority rule and cramdown in depth, the practical difference between secured and unsecured creditor rights and contractual subordination, and the controversial rules governing executive retention pay in bankruptcy.

phases.title: Cross-Border and Out-of-Court Alternatives
phases.description: Understand how Chapter 15 actually recognizes foreign proceedings, how UK Administration, CVAs, and Schemes of Arrangement compare to Chapter 11, and the legal mechanics of restructuring without ever going to court.

phases.title: Working With Counsel
phases.description: Learn how restructuring advisors and lawyers actually divide the work on a live case, the basics of adversary proceedings and bankruptcy litigation, and how to read a first-day declaration and other real case filings.

topics.title: The Automatic Stay — What Freezes the Moment a Case Is Filed
topics.description: Understand exactly what the automatic stay does and doesn't stop the instant a bankruptcy petition is filed, why it's called 'automatic,' and the statutory exceptions and relief-from-stay process that restructuring professionals need to recognize.

steps.t: State Section 362 of the Bankruptcy Code
steps.d: Write one sentence defining the automatic stay: what it stops (collection actions, foreclosures, litigation) and when (instantly upon filing).

Name three claims and creditor actions that the automatic stay does NOT protect against — criminal prosecution, family support obligations, and regulatory agency enforcement — then explain why the Code excludes each.
Write the four steps a secured lender takes to get the stay lifted: the motion, the adequate-protection offer, the debtor's objection, and the equity-in-collateral question the judge decides.

steps.t: Distinguish temporary stay from permanent lifting
steps.d: Explain why a judge might grant 'adequate protection' (temporary stay), letting the case continue, versus lifting the stay entirely (allowing foreclosure), by calculating whether the lender is adequately protected by the debtor's equity and payment capacity.

steps.t: Trace a relief motion through a real case
steps.d: Find a motion for relief from stay on CourtListener and note which lender filed it, over what collateral, and how the judge ruled.

topics.title: Chapters 7, 11, and 15 — Liquidation, Reorganization, and Cross-Border Cases Compared
topics.description: Compare liquidation under Chapter 7, reorganization under Chapter 11, and the ancillary cross-border framework of Chapter 15 — and understand why the choice of chapter shapes everything that follows in a case.

steps.d: Write four sentences explaining Chapter 7: appointment of trustee, asset sale, creditor payments by priority, and discharge.

Explain Chapter 11 in four sentences: the debtor stays in control (debtor-in-possession), management continues operations, creditors form a committee, and a plan is confirmed distributing value to creditors while the company emerges operating.

Define Chapter 15: it provides U.S. recognition of foreign insolvency proceedings and allows coordination when a company with U.S. assets files abroad, typically through a foreign representative petitioning a U.S. court for recognition as 'main' or 'non-main'.
Build a table contrasting Chapter 7, Chapter 11 and Chapter 15 on typical duration, the odds of emerging as a going concern, and cost to creditors.

Write two paragraphs: (1) why a company with strong core operations chooses Chapter 11 instead of Chapter 7 (to keep revenue flowing and maximize value), and (2) why one with no viable operations chooses Chapter 7 (faster, cleaner exit for creditors).

topics.title: Who's in the Room — Debtor's Counsel, the UCC and Its Counsel, the U.S. Trustee, and the Judge
topics.description: Map the actual participants in a Chapter 11 case: debtor's counsel and its fiduciary duties, the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors and its own counsel, the U.S. Trustee's oversight role, and the bankruptcy judge.

steps.t: Define debtor's counsel role and duties
steps.d: Explain whom debtor's counsel represents (the company, not individual creditors) and identify the unique tension when shareholders have no recovery.

steps.t: Describe how the UCC is formed
steps.d: Write down who appoints the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors, who sits on it, the duty it owes, and the two things it most often objects to.

Clarify that UCC counsel is separate from the debtor's counsel and is hired to advise the committee, not the company, creating structural tension that drives negotiations between debtor and creditors.

Define the U.S. Trustee's role (part of DOJ) as the officer who oversees debtor compliance with bankruptcy law, monitors fee applications, and appoints the UCC, but does NOT have the power to directly influence case outcomes.

steps.t: Map participants in a real case
steps.d: Find a first-day declaration from a major case filing (Toys R Us, Bed Bath & Beyond, or similar) and identify each participant mentioned — debtor's counsel firm, UCC counsel, U.S. Trustee district, bankruptcy judge — then list each party's stated objectives.

topics.title: First-Day Motions and the First 30 Days of a Case
topics.description: Learn what first-day motions actually ask for — cash management, critical vendors, wages, utilities — and why the first-day hearing sets the tone for the entire case.

steps.d: From the Troutman or Wall Street Prep article, list six standard first-day motions: cash management, critical vendor orders, wage and benefits, utilities, professional fee retention, and DIP financing authorization — and state the goal of each.

steps.t: Read a cash management motion order
steps.d: Download a first-day order approving cash management from a major Chapter 11 case and identify which pre-petition accounts and credit lines the debtor was authorized to use.

Describe how a debtor identifies vendors whose non-performance would halt operations (key suppliers, utilities, telecom) and seeks court authority to pay pre-petition amounts owed to them immediately, even before other creditors.

Create a calendar showing: filing day (motions due within hours), first-day hearing (24-48 hours), DIP approval, bar date filing (typically 70 days post), claims deadline, and creditor meeting (341 meeting, typically 20-40 days post).
Download the Toys R Us first-day declaration and summarise in one page why it filed, which motions it sought, and what it could not do without same-day authority.

topics.title: DIP Financing Agreements — What's Actually in Them and Why Lenders Get Control
topics.description: Go inside an actual DIP credit agreement: budget covenants, milestones, roll-up provisions, priming liens, and the superpriority status that gives DIP lenders outsized leverage over the case.

steps.t: Read the structure of a DIP agreement
steps.d: Using the Cravath or Weil resource, scan a sample DIP credit agreement and list the main sections: definitions, borrowing base, pricing, covenants, conditions precedent, representations, and remedies.

steps.t: Extract budget covenants from a DIP agreement
steps.d: Read a real DIP credit agreement and identify the approved monthly operating budget, the variance threshold that triggers a default, and what approval is needed to exceed it.

Define priming (DIP lender gets a first lien even ahead of existing secured creditors) and superpriority (unsecured claims status ahead of all other unsecured claims), and explain why these give DIP lenders extraordinary leverage in case negotiations.
Explain in your own words how a DIP lender rolls pre-petition debt into the DIP claim, and why that aligns the lender with confirmation at other creditors' expense.

steps.t: Extract DIP terms from a real case
steps.d: Find a DIP order (authorization) from a recent major Chapter 11 case and summarize: (1) DIP facility size and pricing, (2) three key covenants and the monthly tolerance, (3) priming and superpriority language, and (4) any roll-up provisions.

topics.title: The Plan of Reorganization and Disclosure Statement — From Draft to Confirmation
topics.description: Follow a plan of reorganization from drafting through disclosure statement approval, creditor solicitation, voting, and the confirmation hearing that determines whether a debtor emerges from Chapter 11.

steps.d: List the major steps from plan drafting through confirmation: filing, disclosure statement approval, creditor voting, and confirmation hearing.

steps.t: Write what a disclosure statement is for
steps.d: Explain that a disclosure statement is the document creditors receive before voting on a plan, analogous to a proxy statement in a stock transaction, and must contain all material information creditors need to make an informed vote decision.

From 11 USC § 1129, summarize the mandatory requirements for confirmation: best interests test (creditors receive at least what they would in Chapter 7), feasibility (company can perform the plan), and priority (absolute priority rule is satisfied).

Explain how a plan can be confirmed even if an objecting class votes against it, if other requirements (particularly absolute priority for non-consenting classes) are satisfied — and why this protects equity and junior creditors from senior lender control.
Find a disclosed plan of reorganization on CourtListener and extract the treatment of each creditor class, the going-concern valuation it assumes, and its risk factors.

topics.title: Executory Contracts and Unexpired Leases (Section 365) — Assume, Assign, or Reject
topics.description: Understand the debtor's powerful Section 365 right to cherry-pick which contracts and leases to keep, cure and assume, assign to a third party, or reject — and what that means for counterparties.

steps.t: State Section 365 of the Bankruptcy Code
steps.d: Write one sentence explaining Section 365: what a debtor can do (assume, assign, reject) and when (early in the case).
Write down three executory contracts — an equipment lease, a supply agreement, a licence — and one contract that is not executory, with the reason.
Write out what a debtor must do to assume a contract: cure every pre-petition default and give adequate assurance of future performance, or the counterparty forces rejection.

Explain that assumption keeps the debtor as the contracting party, while assignment transfers the contract to a third party, and describe the anti-assignment default clause common in commercial contracts that restricts assignment without consent.

steps.t: Trace a contract decision in a real case
steps.d: Find a motion to assume or reject contracts in a Chapter 11 docket and note which contracts, the stated rationale, and how the court ruled.

topics.title: Section 363 Sales — Stalking Horse Bids, Auctions, and Selling Assets Free and Clear
topics.description: Learn how a Section 363 sale lets a debtor sell assets outside a plan, free and clear of liens and claims, through a stalking-horse bid, court-supervised auction, and sale hearing.

steps.d: From the Mayer Brown resource, explain that a Section 363 sale allows a debtor to sell substantially all assets outside a plan, free and clear of liens and claims, through a bidding process approved by the court.

steps.t: Pull stalking-horse terms from an order
steps.d: Find a Section 363 sale order and extract: the stalking horse's initial bid, the expense cap or termination fee, and how the auction process is structured.
Lay out the 30-45 day sequence from bid-procedures order to sale hearing, and set it beside how long a normal M&A process takes.
Write down why a § 363 sale passes assets free of liens and claims, and what happens to those liens instead.
Find a § 363 sale order and note the stalking-horse bid, the bids that beat it, the winning price, and whether the secured creditors were made whole.

topics.title: Preferences and Fraudulent Transfers (Sections 547/548) — Clawing Back Pre-Bankruptcy Payments
topics.description: Understand how a trustee or debtor in possession can claw back payments made shortly before filing under the preference rules of Section 547 and the actual and constructive fraud tests of Section 548.

steps.d: Take a payment made 60 days pre-petition and check all five § 547 elements: transfer, creditor, pre-petition debt, timing, and whether the creditor received more than in liquidation.
Write out the five things a trustee must show under § 547, including the 90-day window and that the creditor did better than it would have in a liquidation.

Explain that payments made in the ordinary course of business (e.g., normal supplier payments) are exempt from preference recovery, and that this exception protects operational suppliers from preference suits while liquidating creditors are vulnerable.
Under § 548, write down what makes a transfer constructively fraudulent — less than reasonably equivalent value — and why the lookback is longer than 90 days.

steps.t: Trace a preference or fraudulent transfer claim
steps.d: Find a preference complaint or settlement in a major Chapter 11 case and summarize: (1) the payment or transfer challenged, (2) why the trustee claimed it was a preference or fraud, (3) the defendant's defense, and (4) settlement terms or judgment.

topics.title: The Absolute Priority Rule, From Scratch
topics.description: The waterfall principle the rest of this phase builds on: senior classes paid in full before junior classes get anything.

steps.d: Open 11 U.S.C. § 1129(b) and find the fair-and-equitable test. The rule is two subparagraphs, not a doctrine you have to infer.
Senior secured, junior secured, senior unsecured, subordinated, preferred, common. One line each, in order.
Take a capital structure totalling 100 and an enterprise value of 60, and allocate it down the waterfall until it runs out.
In that example, name the class the value stops at. That class controls the plan, which is why the rule matters commercially.
Note the two ways a junior class can recover anyway: senior classes consent, or the narrow new-value contribution.

topics.title: The Absolute Priority Rule and Cramdown, in Depth
topics.description: Go beyond the one-line definition: study how the absolute priority rule actually gets litigated, what 'fair and equitable' requires class by class, the new value exception, and how a plan gets crammed down over an objecting class.

steps.d: From 11 USC § 1129(b), write the rule: in a cramdown, a non-consenting class receives nothing unless all senior classes are satisfied in full — so equity cannot receive any value if unsecured creditors are not paid in full.
Given a plan treatment for an objecting unsecured creditor class, verify whether it satisfies the Section 1129(b)(2) 'fair and equitable' test for that class.
Write down the one route by which equity keeps a stake despite absolute priority: contributing new money equal to that stake, and note how rarely it succeeds.

Using a capital structure with secured debt, unsecured debt, and equity, walk through a cramdown where unsecured creditors vote no but the plan is confirmed anyway because equity received no recovery (satisfying absolute priority).

steps.t: Analyze a cramdown dispute in a real case
steps.d: Find a confirmation order where absolute priority was contested and note the capital structure, the objection, and how the judge ruled on cramdown.

topics.title: Secured vs. Unsecured Creditor Rights and Contractual Subordination
topics.description: Understand what actually separates a secured claim from an unsecured one in a bankruptcy case, and how contractual subordination agreements between creditors get enforced under Section 510.

steps.d: Define a secured claim (creditor has a lien on collateral) versus unsecured (creditor has no lien), and explain that this distinction determines recovery priority: secured creditors get collateral value first, then unsecured creditors share remaining value.

steps.t: Check lien perfection in a case
steps.d: Take a company balance sheet, identify which liens are noted (mortgages, UCC filings, judgment liens), and verify perfection status against the company's UCC search results.

steps.t: Write out a subordination agreement's effect
steps.d: In two lines, state what creditor B gives up by subordinating to A, and note that § 510 lets a plan reinstate or modify that agreement.

Given a capital structure with senior debt, unsecured debt, and an intercreditor agreement subordinating unsecured debt to senior debt, show how this subordination affects recovery distribution if enterprise value is insufficient to pay senior debt in full.

steps.t: Analyze a subordination dispute in a real case
steps.d: Find a confirmation order involving a contested subordination or lien priority dispute and summarize: (1) which creditor classes disagreed on priority, (2) the subordination or lien documents in question, and (3) how the plan resolved the dispute.

topics.title: Executive Retention Pay in Bankruptcy — KEIP/KERP Rules and Why They're Controversial
topics.description: Learn the BAPCPA-era rules under Section 503(c) that sharply limit retention bonuses (KERPs) but allow incentive plans tied to difficult-to-reach milestones (KEIPs) — and why courts scrutinize the difference so closely.

steps.d: Explain the KERP/KEIP distinction: retention bonuses are capped by statute, while milestone-based incentive plans are allowed but scrutinized for difficulty.
Work out the KERP ceiling for one executive: the lesser of 10% of comparable payments and the statutory dollar cap, and say what that forces the plan to become.

steps.t: Test a milestone for genuine difficulty
steps.d: Take one KEIP milestone and check whether management has historically hit it — the question a court asks to tell an incentive plan from a disguised retention bonus.

steps.t: Map a KEIP vs. KERP decision
steps.d: Given an executive compensation scenario (e.g., $2M retention bonus proposed), explain whether it would qualify as KERP (limited by statute) or KEIP (requires difficult milestones), and calculate the allowed payment.

steps.t: Analyze a contested KERP/KEIP in a real case
steps.d: Find an order on executive retention pay in a Chapter 11 case and note the amount, whether it was a KERP or a KEIP, who objected, and the ruling.

topics.title: Chapter 15 — How Cross-Border Insolvency Actually Works
topics.description: Understand how a foreign representative petitions a U.S. court for recognition of a foreign proceeding as 'main' or 'non-main,' and what powers and protections recognition actually confers.

steps.t: Trace a Chapter 15 petition through recognition
steps.d: Find a Chapter 15 petition in a major cross-border case and identify: the foreign proceeding filed, the recognition sought (main or non-main), the debtor's center of main interests, and the court's ruling.
Write down the three consequences of Chapter 15 recognition: the stay over US assets, the foreign representative's access to US courts, and court-to-court coordination.

Explain that main recognition gives the foreign representative broad control (like a U.S. debtor-in-possession), while non-main recognition is narrower and typically used when U.S. assets are modest or the debtor's main operations are abroad.

Using resources or case law, describe a real-world scenario: a UK company with U.S. subsidiaries and assets files Chapter 15, seeking main recognition for its global proceeding, and explaining how U.S. assets are administered.

steps.t: Apply Chapter 15 mechanics to a scenario
steps.d: For a company incorporated abroad with US assets and US creditors, say whether it files Chapter 15, whether it seeks main or non-main recognition, and why.

topics.title: UK Administration, CVAs, and Schemes of Arrangement — A Working Comparison to Chapter 11
topics.description: Build a working comparison of the major UK restructuring tools — Administration, Company Voluntary Arrangements, Schemes of Arrangement, and the newer Part 26A Restructuring Plan — against U.S. Chapter 11.

steps.d: From the House of Commons Library resource, explain that UK Administration is court-ordered, non-consensual, and faster than Chapter 11: an administrator is appointed, has strict timelines (8 weeks to submit a plan), and can sell assets without creditor vote.

steps.t: Compare CVA voting against Chapter 11 voting
steps.d: Explain why a CVA needs 75% creditor vote (binding on dissenters) while Chapter 11 plans can cramdown with less, and what that means for the company's leverage in negotiation.

steps.t: Place the Part 26A plan against Chapter 11
steps.d: Write down what the UK Restructuring Plan borrows from Chapter 11 and where it differs, including the 75% class vote and its cross-class cramdown.

steps.t: Compare UK and US timelines and outcomes
steps.d: Build a table comparing Chapter 11 (12-36 month average, creditor vote, plan flexibility) versus UK Administration (8-week timeline, administrator discretion, faster asset sales) and CVA/Restructuring Plan (faster if consensual, slower if contested).
Find a company that restructured across both US and UK proceedings and note what was filed where, and why each forum was chosen.

topics.title: Out-of-Court Workouts and Exchange Offers — The Legal Mechanics When You Avoid Court
topics.description: Learn how companies restructure debt entirely outside of bankruptcy court through negotiated workouts and exchange offers, and the securities-law and intercreditor mechanics that make them work.

steps.d: Find a publicly disclosed standstill agreement from a distressed company and extract: the standstill duration, the creditors bound by it, and what actions are prohibited during the standstill.

steps.t: Draft the terms of a standstill
steps.d: Write the three terms any standstill needs: what creditors agree not to do, for how long, and what the debtor must deliver during it.
Write down what the debtor offers, what creditors give up, the acceptance threshold, and why no court is involved.
Write down which exemption a distressed exchange relies on — Rule 144A or Regulation S — and what that limits about who can participate.

Build a decision tree: when would out-of-court workouts succeed (simple capital structure, good faith creditors, time to negotiate) versus when would Chapter 11 be necessary (complex structure, creditor disagreement, need for cramdown)?

topics.title: How Restructuring Advisors and Lawyers Actually Divide the Work
topics.description: Understand the practical division of labor on a real case between debtor's counsel, the investment bank or turnaround consultant, and the chief restructuring officer — and how the best teams coordinate.

steps.d: List the typical participants: debtor's counsel (negotiations, plan drafting), restructuring bank (valuation, DIP negotiations, plan sponsors), turnaround consultant (operations, CRO role), and sometimes specialized advisors (tax, labor, environmental).

Explain that a Chief Restructuring Officer (often from a consulting firm) is hired by the debtor to oversee operations and plan strategy, answering to the board/existing management but with fiduciary duty to maximize enterprise value.

steps.t: Identify CRO appointment and scope in a case
steps.d: From a first-day order, find the CRO appointment and list the operational decisions (store closures, headcount cuts, vendor selection) explicitly granted to the CRO alone.

steps.t: Write down how the team coordinates
steps.d: Name who decides operations, who decides legal strategy, and how the professionals' fees being paid from plan proceeds aligns them on emergence.

steps.t: Analyze team dynamics in a real case
steps.d: Find a first-day hearing order and identify debtor's counsel, the restructuring advisor, any CRO, and which decisions each appears to own.

topics.title: Adversary Proceedings and Bankruptcy Litigation Basics
topics.description: Learn what turns a bankruptcy case into a lawsuit: the categories of disputes that must be filed as adversary proceedings under Rule 7001, and how that litigation track runs alongside the main case.

steps.t: State Rule 7001 types of adversary proceedings
steps.d: List the main categories of adversary proceedings: property disputes, counterclaims, avoidance actions (preferences and fraud), and discharge injunctions.
For one dispute, say whether it belongs in a contested motion or a separate adversary proceeding, and name the factor that decides it.
Write down the differences in forum, procedure and discovery between a contested motion in the main case and an adversary proceeding.

Name three common adversary proceedings: (1) preference suits by trustee against creditors, (2) discharge injunction disputes (creditor alleges debtor committed fraud), (3) confirmation plan objections (requires full litigation if contested).

Find an adversary proceeding complaint filed in a major Chapter 11 case and summarize: (1) plaintiff and defendant, (2) legal claim (preference, fraud, contract, priority), (3) relief sought, and (4) whether it was settled or litigated to judgment.

topics.title: Reading a First-Day Declaration and Other Real Case Filings
topics.description: Read an actual first-day declaration from a major, well-documented Chapter 11 case and learn how to extract the business history, capital structure, and narrative that every other filing in the case builds on.

steps.d: Download the first-day declaration from Toys R Us Chapter 11 (provided in resources) or a comparable recent major case and read the full text.
From the declaration, note the company's business and revenue model, how it performed historically, and the change that caused the distress.

From the declaration, list the major debt tranches, secured lenders, unsecured creditors, and equity holders named, and calculate approximate percentages of total enterprise value represented by each.

Analyze how the declaration frames the company's distress: Is it blamed on external factors (pandemic, industry disruption) or internal mismanagement? Does this framing affect which creditor classes the debtor will ask for concessions?
Compare declarations from two major cases on: business model, stated cause of distress, capital structure, and how the debtor frames the narrative.
